title-group.article-title: Dietary fat is associated with increased inflammatory bowel disease onset risk: a systematic review and dose–response meta-analysis

sec.title: Background and aims:
sec.p: The association between dietary fat and the risk of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) onset, especially for specific fatty acids, is controversial. We aimed to examine and quantify the association between dietary fat and IBD onset risk.

sec.title: Methods:
sec.p: PubMed, Embase and Web of Science were searched for studies that reported estimates of IBD onset risk up to January 2025. Relative risks (RRs) and 95% CIs were pooled, and subgroup analyses, meta-regression, and evaluations of dose‒response relationships were conducted.

sec.title: Results:
sec.p: High fat intake (RR = 1.24, 95% CI = 1.03–1.49) was modestly associated with increased IBD onset risk. Subgroup analyses and meta-regression indicated that Asian (RR = 2.15, 95% CI = 1.46–3.16, Psubgroup < 0.01), high-male-proportion (RR = 1.91, 95% CI = 1.32–2.78, Psubgroup < 0.01) and young (RR = 2.67, 95% CI = 1.80–3.96, Psubgroup < 0.01) populations were more susceptible to fat-associated IBD, and positive dose‒response associations were also confirmed in these populations. Both the highest-versus-lowest and dose‒response analyses revealed that polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) (RR = 1.34, 95% CI = 1.10–1.63; Pnonlinearity < 0.05; per 10 g/day RR = 1.39) and cholesterol (RR = 1.52, 95% CI = 1.09-2.12; Pnonlinearity = 0.03; per 0.1 g/day RR = 1.17) were associated with increased IBD onset risk, whereas long-chain n-3 PUFA (LCN-n-3, RR = 0.74, 95% CI = 0.58–0.94) intake and a high n3/n6-PUFA ratio (RR = 0.76, 95% CI = 0.59–0.98) might be associated with decreased IBD risk.

sec.title: Conclusions:
sec.p: Higher fat intake might be modestly associated with increased IBD onset risk, particularly for PUFA and cholesterol, whereas LCN-n-3 and a high n3/n6-PUFA ratio may offer protective effects against IBD onset.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), which includes ulcerative colitis (UC) and Crohn’s disease (CD), affects nearly 0.3% of the global population, more than 20 million people[1]. While the incidence of IBD remains stable in developed countries, it has increased continually in most developing countries, where a Westernized diet is becoming increasingly prevalent. Several clinical guidelines on IBD nutrition advocate low consumption of saturated fatty acids (SFAs) and high intake of n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs)[2,3], but there is considerable variability regarding the optimal amount and types of fat consumed, reflecting uncertainties in the current evidence.

High fat intake has long been linked to an increased risk of IBD onset; however, subsequent studies failed to confirm a positive association[4–7], which might be weakened or confounded by female sex only, a limited number of IBD patients and regional differences. A previous systematic review examined the relationship between dietary fat and IBD risk but was based on a limited sample size and did not include a quantitative analysis[8]. More importantly, various types of fatty acids may have opposing effects on IBD onset; however, no meta-analyses have been conducted to assess their individual effects quantitatively, let alone to illustrate dose‒response associations. Therefore, our study aimed to evaluate the association between fat intake (including specific fatty acids) and IBD onset risk, with dose‒response analyses conducted to quantify the risk. All the use of generative AI in the article complies with the TITAN guidelines[9].

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: We adopted the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses (PRISMA)[10], Meta-analysis of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (MOOSE)[11] statement and Assessing the methodological quality of systematic reviews (AMSTAR) tool[12] as guidance for reporting the systematic review. We systematically searched all studies up to 31 January 2025, in the PubMed, Embase and Web of Science databases, with no language limitations. Prospective observational cohort and case‒control studies were included if they reported the relative risk (RR) or odds ratio (OR) with a 95% confidence interval (CI) for the associations between fat intake (including fatty acids) and IBD onset. Two reviewers (S.Z. and M.L.) independently screened the titles and abstracts of the articles, reviewed the full text and made decisions for inclusion and subsequent data extraction and quality assessment.

The ORs and RRs (with 95% CIs) for the highest versus lowest categories of total fat and fatty acids were calculated using Orsini’s method. Publication bias was assessed by Egger’s test and visual inspection of enhanced funnel plots. A sensitivity analysis was performed by excluding each study individually to determine its impact on the overall effect. Subgroup analyses were conducted to identify potential heterogeneity on the basis of prespecified subgroups. Both nonlinear and linear dose‒response analyses were also conducted to confirm the association and quantify IBD onset risk with a fixed fat increment. The detailed methodology, including the search strategy, is provided in Supplemental Material Digital Content, available at: http://links.lww.com/JS9/E868

list-item.p: First meta-analysis to comprehensively evaluate the association between fat (including fatty acid) intake and IBD onset risk; High-fat diet slightly increased the IBD onset risk, and each 10 g increment was associated with 5% increased risk.
The Asian, male and young populations were more susceptible to fat-associated IBD.
The effects of specific fatty acids on IBD onset risk were heterogenized, where a high n3/n6-PUFA ratio and long-chain n-3 PUFA level may protect population against IBD onset.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Ultimately, 15 out of the 6,869 studies that met the inclusion criteria were included in this meta-analysis (Supplemental Digital Content Figure 1, available at: http://links.lww.com/JS9/E868), the detailed search strategy and characteristics of included studies are presented in Supplemental Digital Content Tables 1–5 (available at: http://links.lww.com/JS9/E868). According to the Newcastle‒Ottawa Scale, 12 of the 15 included studies were deemed high quality (Supplemental Digital Content Table 6, available at: http://links.lww.com/JS9/E868). Fat intake in all studies was assessed using a food frequency questionnaire (FFQ).

sec.title: Meta-analysis of fat and IBD
sec.p: The meta-analysis comparing the highest-versus lowest fat intake showed that the RR for IBD onset risk was 1.24 (95% CI = 1.03–1.49, I2 = 24%, n = 17); the RRs for the risk of UC and CD were 1.24 (95% CI = 0.99–1.57; I2 = 29%; n = 10) and 1.23 (95% CI = 0.91–1.66; I2 = 30%; n = 7), respectively (Figs. 1 and 2). Consistent results were observed in both positive linear dose‒response association and dose‒response effect (LDE) analyses (Plinearity = 0.04; per 10 g/day RR = 1.047; 95% CI = 1.001-1.096; I2 = 25%; n = 14; Fig. 3). No significant publication bias was detected in either the enhanced funnel plot (Supplemental Digital Content Figure 2, available at: http://links.lww.com/JS9/E868) or Egger’s test (P = 0.09). The sensitivity analysis indicated that excluding any single study did not materially alter the pooled RR (Supplemental Digital Content Figure 3, available at: http://links.lww.com/JS9/E868).

Subgroup analyses indicated that the associations between fat intake and IBD onset risk were more robust in Asian populations (RR = 2.15; 95% CI = 1.46–3.16; I2 = 34%; n = 4; Psubgroup < 0.01), high-male-proportion (RR = 1.91; 95% CI = 1.32–2.78; I2 = 15%; n = 8; Psubgroup < 0.01) and young populations (RR = 2.67; 95% CI = 1.80–3.96; I2 = 0%; n = 6; Psubgroup < 0.01; Fig. 2; Supplemental Digital Content Figures 4–6, available at: http://links.lww.com/JS9/E868). Consistent results were observed in Asian populations (Pnonlinearity = 0.009; per 10 g/day RR = 1.19; 95% CI = 1.08–1.31; I2 = 16%; n = 5), high-male-proportion (Pnonlinearity = 0.005; per 10 g/day RR = 1.14; 95% CI = 1.04–1.25; I2 = 12%; n = 7) and young populations (Pnonlinearity < 0.001; per 10 g/day RR = 1.20; 95% CI = 1.10–1.31; I2 = 0%; n = 5; Fig. 3; Supplemental Digital Content Figures 7–10; Supplemental Digital Content Table 7, available at: http://links.lww.com/JS9/E868) in both nonlinear dose‒response associations and LDE analysis.

sec.title: Meta-analysis of specific fatty acids and IBD
sec.p: The intake of mono–unsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs) was associated with increased IBD onset risk in the highest-versus-lowest analysis (RR = 1.62; 95% CI = 1.14–2.29; I2 = 59%; n = 10; Fig. 2; Supplemental Digital Content Figure 11, available at: http://links.lww.com/JS9/E868) but not in the dose‒response association or LDE analysis (Fig. 3; Supplemental Digital Content Figures 12 and 13, available at: http://links.lww.com/JS9/E868). However, PUFA intake was linked to an increased risk of IBD onset in the highest-versus-lowest groups (RR = 1.34; 95% CI = 1.10–1.63; I2 = 40%; n = 10; Fig. 2), and a dose‒response analysis was performed (Pnonlinearity < 0.05; per 10 g/day RR = 1.39; 95% CI = 1.05–1.83; I2 = 41%; n = 9; Fig. 3; Supplemental Digital Content Figures 14 and 15, available at: http://links.lww.com/JS9/E868). Similarly, cholesterol intake showed consistent findings in the highest-versus-lowest ratio (RR = 1.52; 95% CI = 1.09–2.12; I2 = 33%; n = 7; Fig. 2) and dose‒response analysis (Pnonlinearity = 0.03; per 0.1 g/day RR = 1.17; 95% CI = 1.02-1.35; I2 = 12%; n = 6; Fig. 3; Supplemental Digital Content Figures 16 and 17, available at: http://links.lww.com/JS9/E868).

Notably, the n3/n6-PUFA ratio was associated with a reduced IBD onset risk in both the highest-versus-lowest (RR = 0.76; 95% CI = 0.59–0.98; I2 = 0%; n = 3; Fig. 2) and dose‒response associations (P < 0.05; n = 3; Fig. 3; Supplemental Digital Content Figures 18 and 19, available at: http://links.lww.com/JS9/E868). Increased long-chain n-3 PUFA (LCN-n-3) intake was linked to a decreased IBD risk in the highest-versus-lowest (RR = 0.74; 95% CI = 0.58–0.94; I2 = 0%; n = 4; Fig. 2; Supplemental Digital Content Figure 20, available at: http://links.lww.com/JS9/E868) and LDE analyses (per 0.1 g/day RR = 0.47; 95% CI = 0.24–0.89; n = 1; Fig. 3). No significant associations between other fatty acids and IBD onset risk were found (Supplemental Digital Content Figures 12 and 21–40, available at: http://links.lww.com/JS9/E868). Consistent findings were observed in specific analyses of the association between UC and CD onset risk (Supplemental Digital Content Figures 41–83; Supplemental Digital Content Table 8, available at: http://links.lww.com/JS9/E868). Details with the citation codes of the included studies are provided in Supplemental Digital Content.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: To our knowledge, this is the first meta-analysis to comprehensively quantify the positive association between fat (including fatty acid) intake and IBD onset risk, where three specific populations (Asian, male and young) were found to be more susceptible to fat-associated IBD. On the basis of data from over 500 000 individuals and 1800 IBD patients, our study demonstrated that high fat intake might be associated with a modest increase in IBD onset risk (RR = 1.24), the magnitude of which is similar to that reported in other meta-analyses on IBD risk factors (such as higher intake of meat: RR = 1.50, 95% CI = 1.15–1.95[13]) and approximately twice that reported in Asian (RR = 2.15), male (RR = 1.91) and young (RR = 2.67) populations, all of which were confirmed by dose‒response analyses. Among fatty acids, PUFAs and cholesterol were associated with 34% and 52% increased IBD onset risk, respectively, whereas LCN-n-3 (RR = 0.74) and a high n3/n6-PUFA ratio (RR = 0.76) had protective effects.

The incidence of IBD is highest in industrialized nations and continues to increase when nations become more industrialized, leading to the hypothesis that westernization, particularly the Western diet, may be a key trigger for IBD[14]. Recent randomized controlled trials have shown the protective role of reducing fat intake[15] and other similar dietary interventions[16] in reducing IBD risk; thus, a new dietary intervention policy for reducing fat intake should be introduced to reduce the high incidence of IBD, especially in young, male, and Asian populations.

However, limitations still exist. The role of residual confounding resulting from unmeasured factors (such as the intake of fiber, sugar and ultra-processed foods) or unknown factors cannot be entirely excluded, which may affect the results. The inclusion of all observational studies limited the ability to analyze the causal association between a high-fat diet and IBD risk. Given the limited number of studies for certain subgroups, the results might be uncertain owing to regional dietary patterns and diverse genetic backgrounds, which should be validated in future randomized trials. Additionally, more nuanced types of fatty acids and the risk of IBD onset are rarely reported, making it difficult to assess such associations.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In conclusion, our findings demonstrated a modest positive association between fat intake and IBD onset risk and identified three susceptible subpopulations in fat-associated IBD, which might be valuable for developing preventive strategies for IBD. Significant heterogeneity in the effects of specific fatty acids on IBD onset risk was also revealed, where a high n3/n6-PUFA ratio and LCN-n-3 level were found to reduce IBD onset, indicating the need for investigations on the individual mechanism of specific fatty acids, although more studies are still needed, especially for specific populations and fatty acids.
